purpose: Expose the release architecture through a clear CLI and portable CI contract, and migrate Callisto's GitHub Actions release workflow to an artifact-bound, Environment-gated execution job without preserving legacy mutation bypasses.
scope: The release CLI command family, legacy-command transition, user-facing state-path and artifact inputs, GitHub Actions plan/build/execute topology, managed release-PR continuity, workflow permissions and action pinning, and documentation needed to operate the new flow. Provider-neutral planning, capability validation, state, and effects are owned by predecessor specs and consumed here.
non_goals: Making GitHub Actions the only supported CI provider or moving core release authority into workflow shell scripts.
Allowing a command-line flag, environment variable, CI cache, inline JSON, or workflow input to bypass release intent validation, Git trust, artifact verification, or ApplyPermit.
Keeping legacy publish/tag mutation behavior indefinitely.

command_contract.release plan: Read-only. Local use derives a decision from exact qualified package selections. CI uses an explicit merged-release-commit mode to interpret the immutable parent-to-merged Callisto release-PR delta, verify the consumed changesets and version/changelog closure, and embed the result in a transient intent. It does not rerun changeset planning after merge and it neither publishes, tags, pushes, nor creates a forge release.
command_contract.release inspect: Read-only. Displays an intent, artifact manifest, state, or receipt with their binding and readiness checks; it does not recompute an unapproved intent as a side effect.
command_contract.release execute: The sole production mutation entry point. It consumes explicit intent and, when needed, artifact-manifest inputs, validates them, obtains a fresh ValidatedReleaseIntent and ApplyPermit, and runs the coordinator from SPEC-RELEASE-EXECUTION-012.
command_contract.release reconcile: Read-only. Consumes explicit intent/state inputs and performs exact provider observations to report recoverability; it never publishes, tags, pushes, or creates a forge release.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: Callisto exposes `release plan`, `release inspect`, `release execute`, and `release reconcile` as explicitly named commands or an equally explicit namespaced interface with the four contracts above. `release plan` requires repeated exact qualified package selections or one named documented configuration-selection mode and embeds the resulting decision in the intent. `release execute` requires an explicit intent file path; it never searches the checkout, falls back to a default plan, accepts an inline JSON authority string, accepts a new selection, or recomputes a plan after validation fails. It accepts an explicit artifact-manifest path when the intent declares binary slots, and an optional explicit state path; omitting the latter uses SPEC-RELEASE-EXECUTION-012's outside-checkout default. Parse, trust, binding, capability, artifact, attestation, or state validation failures exit non-zero before credentials or mutating adapters are reached.

`release plan`, `release inspect`, and `release reconcile` are structurally read-only: their reachable command paths cannot call registry publish, Git tag/push, forge-release creation, or any provider effect adapter. `release execute` is structurally the only production CLI route that can acquire an ApplyPermit and dispatch those adapters. Integration tests invoke every command against recording adapters and assert the exact allowed effect set, including that each error path dispatches none.

During the documented migration window, `plan-publish`, `publish`, `tag --plan`, and `filter-plan` remain available only as clearly labelled read-only compatibility previews. They may render proposed operations but cannot publish, tag, push, write release state, create a forge release, or acquire ApplyPermit. Their help and diagnostics name `release plan`, `release execute`, or `release reconcile` as the replacement as appropriate. A separately documented breaking release removes the legacy commands rather than silently restoring their mutation behavior.

The repository has a separate least-privilege version-PR flow and a GitHub release workflow with separate plan, build, and execute jobs. The version-PR flow recomputes the generated version/changelog/consumed-changeset delta from the current base branch rather than rebasing a prior generated commit; normally it creates or updates one stable managed release PR and removes exactly the consumed changesets only in that PR. The flow updates the managed branch through the forge's commit API rather than a local `git push`, specifically so the built-in token never needs to write `.github/workflows/*` on any ref: it stages the generated change as a commit rooted at the current base via `createCommitOnBranch` on a deterministic staging branch, then moves the managed branch's ref onto that commit with a plain REST ref update. A managed branch already replaced under the prior SHA-suffixed fallback (a `--<sha>` suffix) remains a trusted, ordinary managed branch and continues to be updated in place. This requires no elevated token, never removes changesets from the base branch, and trusts only the canonical managed branch or an exact SHA-suffixed replacement branch from the repository itself. An optional App or fine-grained token may retain the same PR number but is never required for the default flow. The unprivileged release-plan job checks out the exact merged release commit and its parent, proves the reviewed release delta, runs only read-only merged-release-commit planning, and uploads the transient intent file plus its SHA-256 as same-run workflow artifacts. The build job consumes that exact intent, builds the declared binary slots from the matching source commit, verifies its own intent digest, creates a GitHub artifact attestation for each binary with `attestations: write` and `id-token: write` only in that job, and uploads the artifact manifest and binaries as workflow artifacts. The privileged execute job downloads only artifacts from the same workflow run, independently verifies the intent SHA-256, source commit, artifact-manifest bindings, downloaded binary digests, and each binary's GitHub attestation against the configured repository and immutable signer workflow before invoking `release execute`. No decision or intent is committed or recovered from a cache. A plan/build/execute/attestation mismatch fails before registry, Git, or forge credentials are available.

The GitHub execute job is the only job with release secrets or write-scoped token permissions and is bound to a named GitHub Environment with required reviewers and branch/tag deployment rules. Workflow documentation states the environment name and an administrator-verifiable procedure to confirm its live protection rules; a CI/setup check queries GitHub's API and rejects an environment without non-empty required reviewers. Workflow YAML alone is not evidence that the gate is configured. Planning/build jobs use read-only or no token permissions and receive neither registry nor forge credentials.

Every workflow/job declares least-privilege permissions. Third-party GitHub Actions are pinned to immutable full commit SHAs with nearby upstream-release comments, and an automated policy check rejects mutable action tags or branches. CODEOWNERS plus branch protection requires designated review for changes under `.github/workflows/` and `.github/actions/`. Caches may accelerate dependency installation but cannot carry an intent, state, receipt, artifact manifest, artifact bytes, or authority across jobs/runs.

The CLI reference and release-operation documentation provide one end-to-end local and CI recovery flow: create intent from a clean detached checkout; inspect it; build/produce the intent-bound artifact manifest when binaries are declared; execute with an optional explicit state path; reconcile after interruption. Documentation distinguishes source crate publishes from compiled binary uploads, explains that local default state is outside the checkout, and never instructs users to commit state or use GitHub cache for release authority/recovery.

implementation_notes: The composite action may be retained for non-privileged setup or read-only operations, but it cannot by itself enforce the plan/build/Environment-gated job boundary. The repository workflow must express that boundary.

The artifact handoff is transport, not approval. The execute job repeats cryptographic and semantic binding checks in the Callisto CLI before adapter construction. GitHub artifact attestations prove build provenance for the binary bytes; the intent and manifest additionally prove those bytes are the assets this release approved.

Other CI providers can implement the same explicit-file contract: immutable intent digest, exact source checkout, manifest-plus-byte verification, state artifact, and a separately protected execute credential boundary.
revision_note:
Split from umbrella SPEC-RELEASE-EXECUTION-FOUNDATION-007 to keep user/CI entry points and GitHub-specific controls dependent on a settled provider-neutral execution contract. Amended to make the managed release-PR reconstruction contract explicit and to provide a zero-configuration, SHA-suffixed fallback for GitHub's workflow-ref permission restriction.

Amended again after empirical testing against the real orin-dx/callisto public repository showed the SHA-suffixed fallback masked, rather than fixed, GitHub's workflow-permission restriction, causing visible PR churn. AC-004 now describes the forge-commit-API approach (see SPEC-RELEASE-PR-DECISION-014) that avoids the restriction entirely instead of working around it with a replacement branch.
